title_en: FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns
excerpt_en: The post FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: A scientist tests generic drugs at the Connecticut-based lab Valisure. Tonje Thielesen for ProPublica The Food and Drug Administration will test more prescription drugs for impurities and other dangerous quality lapses under an expanded program described by safety experts as a critical step to better protecting America’s drug supply.

About 90% of prescriptions in the United States are for generic drugs, many manufactured thousands of miles away in countries that include India and China. Until now, the FDA has only periodically tested a sampling of those drugs to see if they were safe or worked as effectively as the brand-name medications they are meant to replicate.
Look Up Where Your Generic Prescription Drugs Were Made Last week, the FDA announced it will test more often and identify poorly performing drugs for further study.

The agency said it will buy the medications from retail pharmacies and wholesale distributors, but it did not say how many drugs it plans to test or how frequently. A spokesperson did not answer questions about how the FDA would select drugs for testing or how it would hold manufacturers accountable for inferior products, beyond posting the results on its website. Still, drug-safety experts said the expansion helps address long-standing concerns that some suppliers sacrifice quality to keep costs low — and that the FDA has for years looked the other way.
“All drugs, regardless of where they are manufactured, must meet the same FDA standards for safety, effectiveness and quality,” the FDA spokesperson told ProPublica.

A ProPublica investigation last year found the agency routinely relied on the drug companies themselves to do their own testing even as doctors, researchers and the Department of Defense warned that essential medications were contaminated or ineffective. On its website, the FDA said it has relied on a “more targeted, risk-based” approach to testing since 2018, choosing samples of drugs that have safety, effectiveness or quality concerns. The agency publicly reports the results on its website and notes that a majority of the tested drugs meet its standards.

ProPublica, however, found the agency for years failed to regularly test both the generics that have worried outside experts and drugs coming from factories that amassed so many serious quality and safety violations they were ultimately banned from the U.S. market. ProPublica later used FDA data to create Rx Inspector, a first-of-its-kind tool that allows consumers and doctors to look up the inspection records of the factories where more than 40,000 generic drugs are made.

Researchers have repeatedly urged the FDA to test more often. In fiscal year 2025, the FDA reported testing 46 different drugs, and for 29 of those drugs, the agency only tested one manufacturer. All but one passed every test.

The FDA’s new testing regime is “a huge validation of the research that we’ve been doing raising concerns about the quality of generic drugs,” Dr. Kevin Schulman, a professor of medicine and health policy at Stanford University, said of the FDA’s new testing program. “This is a great effort on their part.”
In February, senators also introduced a bill targeting transparency in the drug supply chain process, in part because of similar public concerns.

In response to questions about how it would decide which drugs to sample and how results would drive future enforcement, the FDA spokesperson said the initiative will “help the FDA identify potential drug quality issues faster and will provide more information the agency can use to decide if further action is needed.”

Experts say they ultimately hope the FDA’s program will work alongside independent testers to shift the generic drug market to be competitive on quality rather than price. While the agency can focus on weeding out the worst actors, independent labs can test manufacturers against one another to find the most effective products, said retired Col. Vic Suarez, a former medical supply-chain commander. A similar system is already used at the Department of Defense.

“It’s an important thing because they will probably catch extreme violators of regulatory standards, so that’s a good thing,” Suarez said. “But you also need to have a complementary system where you’re actually raising the bar.”

ProPublica previously engaged an independent lab, Valisure, to test several generic versions of three of the most prescribed drugs in the United States and in two cases identified irregularities that experts said could compromise their effectiveness.
“I think, high level, the idea that we should be doing more testing is fantastic,” said David Light, the co-founder of Valisure. “I think there’s so much growing energy behind that.”
The post FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns appeared first on ProPublica.

title_en: Ukraine war briefing: Stop using tear gas on battlefield, dozens of countries tell Russia
excerpt_en: Call comes after chemical weapons watchdog confirms traces of riot-control agent found in Kyiv trench hit with Russian grenade. What we know on day 1,737
body_en: Officials from 34 countries and the EU have called on Russia to stop using riot-control gas on the ⁠battlefield, after the global chemical weapons watchdog confirmed that Ukraine had found traces of teargas in a trench Kyiv said was hit with ⁠a Russian grenade. The joint statement was issued on Wednesday in response to a Ukrainian report circulated to 193 countries as the Organisation ‌for the Prohibition of Chemical ‌Weapons (OPCW) gathered in The Hague this week. Ukraine said it had documented more than 14,000 ‌cases of munitions filled with riot-control agents and toxic chemicals used by Russia on the frontline since 2022. The OPCW said “designated laboratories” approved by the watchdog had “confirmed the presence of a riot-control agent (CS) in samples collected at the scene”.

Riot-control agents such as CS, a form of teargas, are banned in warfare. “We call for the immediate cessation of the use of any toxic chemicals and of ⁠riot control agents as a method of warfare in Ukraine,” non-proliferation directors from Britain, France, Germany, Japan, New Zealand and the EU, among others, said in a statement. News reports midyear said western intelligence had found that Russian forces were using riot-control agents to drive Ukrainian troops out of trenches and into the open so they could fire on them. Russia has denied using illegal munitions, and has accused Ukraine of doing so.

Russian forces attacked Kyiv with ballistic ⁠missiles late on Wednesday, striking a shopping centre and two other ⁠buildings, mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Two ⁠sets of loud explosions were heard. Klitschko said the ‌attack was ongoing, and warned residents to ‌remain in shelters. Three people were wounded, with one in a serious condition.

Ukrainian forces struck a major airbase in Russia, damaging ⁠five planes used to launch missiles and bombs at Ukraine, the Ukrainian general staff said. Russia ⁠did not immediately ⁠comment on Wednesday’s claim, which said the Savasleyka airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region had been hit in Kyiv’s latest long-range attack. Three MiG-31 jets and two Su-34 fighter-bombers were knocked out of operation “for some time”, the general ‌staff said.

German chancellor Friedrich Merz accused Russia of “escalating” threats to European security as he defended ⁠his government’s plans to ⁠bolster defence spending and maintain financial aid to Ukraine. Opposition parties, including on the far right and hard left, have called for an end to aid to Kyiv. “It ⁠cannot be said often enough, against the far right as much as the far left: Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine,” Merz told the Bundestag. “Russia is escalating in the Baltic region, in Poland, on the Black Sea; Russia is escalating in space, and Russia is by now also escalating ‌massively here in our own ‌country.”

US envoy Jared Kushner has warned against a downward spiral in the Ukraine conflict, which he called “a proxy war where Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia”. He told a German podcast that “it won’t take a lot of miscalculation for this thing to escalate massively”. Kushner also appeared to accuse the Europeans of hypocrisy for continuing to buy Russian energy while backing Ukraine.

Poland will create a no-fly zone near the Ukrainian border, a deputy defence minister has announced, after several incursions into its airspace, which it blamed on Russia. The no-fly zone is intended to allow Polish forces to quickly identify any Russian military aircraft and shoot them down if necessary.

Preparations for Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian utility infrastructure this winter are a top priority for the government, a Russian deputy prime minister said. “This ‌is now the most important question: how we’ll get through the winter, especially given drone attacks, particularly in the border regions,” Marat Khusnullin told lawmakers on Wednesday.

Nine more Ukrainian children have been reunited with ⁠their families amid the war in Ukraine, bringing the total to 43, under an ⁠initiative led by ⁠US first lady Melania Trump, the White House and Russia said on Wednesday. There was no immediate comment from Ukrainian authorities.

title_en: Recent sinking of Russian vessels abroad shows the Russia-Ukraine war has officially gone global
excerpt_en: For Ukraine to have any chance of winning the war against Russia, it must increase the pressure on Vladimir Putin’s government. Making Russian assets vulnerable globally is one way to do it.
body_en: Ukraine has been executing a series of successful strikes against Russian assets around the world. Ukrainian forces disabled a Russian cargo vessel off the coast of Finland, and sunk a Russian corvette, the Merkury, along with damaging another cargo vessel, in Libyan waters.
These attacks, in the aftermath of Ukraine’s severe damage to the Kerch Strait Bridge in Russian-occupied Crimea, have created hope among Ukraine’s allies.

The year 2026 hasn’t advanced Ukraine’s goal of ending the war. A stagnant battlefront, increased Russian aerial attacks and a recalcitrant American president have increased the burdens on Ukraine’s government and its people.
Russia hasn’t had a good year either. More than 400,000 Russians have been killed in the war — and potentially as many as 700,000.
For Ukraine to have any chance of winning, it must increase the pressure on Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s government. Making Russian assets vulnerable globally is one way to do it.

The international dimension Since its outset, the Russia-Ukraine conflict has had an international dimension. Ukraine’s allies, both prior to and after Russia’s full-fledged invasion in 2022, rushed supplies to Ukraine in its moment of need.
Providing aid to Ukraine has continued for the past four years, despite disruptions caused by United States President Donald Trump’s involvement in the negotiation process.

The supplies provided by Ukraine’s allies are critical to its success. While the fighting is conducted by the Ukrainian people and Ukraine has increased domestic arms production, outside supplies are crucial in a number of areas — notably, air defence.

Equally important is the economic aid Ukraine’s allies have and continue to provide the country. Given the size differential between Russia and Ukraine and how hard the war has hit the Ukrainian economy, economic aid allows Ukraine to provide basic services to its citizens.

Initially, Russia did not court outside support to the same extent as Ukraine, as it believed it would achieve a rapid victory over its adversary. Once the reality of the conflict became clear, Russia turned to the international community for support.
That support has taken many forms. Iran and North Korea have been among Russia’s top supporters, providing drones and soldiers.

Other countries, most notably China, have provided an economic lifeline to Russia, allowing it access to their markets in an effort to stave off the worst impacts of the economic sanctions Ukraine’s allies have imposed on the Russians.
Countries in Central Asia and the Middle East have also served Russia as important intermediaries for acquiring sanctioned materials.

Targeting support In a conflict that is increasingly defined by attrition, it’s been necessary for both Ukraine and Russia to rally their allies. The demands of industrialized warfare and the production of necessary armaments means neither country can produce what’s needed on their own.

Because both sides are receiving critical support in this industrialized conflict, the war has reached an equilibrium. In their current states, neither side is likely to achieve a decisive breakthrough to rapidly end the fighting.
For both Ukraine and Russia, that means targeting their adversary’s international allies is necessary to win the conflict.
The least risky form of targeting enemy support, and among the most important, is by constructing narratives while delegitimizing those of your opponent.

Ukraine has focused on Russia’s aggression and its violation of international norms and laws. The focus on international law is particularly important for Ukraine given Russian accusations that the West has flouted international norms for decades; Russia uses western association with Ukraine to gain support in the Global South.

Russia has put forward several narratives to justify the war, ranging from defending itself from NATO imperialist expansion to its factually questionable claims of the Ukrainian state’s genocide against ethnic Russians in Ukraine.
Russia had some early successes from these narratives, making political gains in Africa and earning support among far-right European parties.

Narrative campaigns, however, typically unfold over a long time frame. As both Ukraine and Russia seek immediate ways to boost morale and undermine their adversary, direct military operations abroad have become all the more significant.

title_en: Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul
excerpt_en: The post Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: A D.C.-area train commuter photographed a White House staffer’s laptop and notes, which showed a draft plan for the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History. Photo illustration by Jovelle Tamayo/ProPublica. Source images: obtained by ProPublica, Elizabeth Frantz for ProPublica. A top congressional Democrat announced she will investigate the Trump White House’s potential overhaul of the leadership and curatorial decisions at the Smithsonian Institution, the independent agency that oversees 21 national museums.

In a letter sent on Tuesday to the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, cited ProPublica’s recent story on the draft plans by a White House staffer targeting one of the Smithsonian’s most prominent museums, calling the reporting “extremely concerning.”

Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul Pingree, who is slated to lead the subcommittee that controls the Smithsonian’s funding in the next Congress, said the plans revealed in the ProPublica story align with the administration’s broader efforts to interfere with the Smithsonian, which receives federal funding but is governed by a 17-person Board of Regents whose members include the chief justice of the United States, members of Congress, the vice president and private citizens.

In an interview with ProPublica, Pingree said that she intended her letter to put the Smithsonian governing board on notice that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress is monitoring the institution to make sure the board upholds its responsibility to keep the agency independent from political pressure.

“No White House employee riding on the Metro gets to design a plan for what future exhibits look like or gets to veto staffers or exhibits at the Smithsonian,” Pingree said. “That’s not how it works.”

Pingree told ProPublica that she plans to use her powers as chair in the next Congress to aggressively look into what she called the Trump administration’s meddling with the Smithsonian and to expose those efforts to the broader American public.
“We fully intend to dig deeper than has been done in the past,” she said.

Pingree’s letter comes in response to ProPublica reporting on a 25-item list of possible changes that, taken together, would amount to an unprecedented attempt by the White House to control the content and personnel of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, which attracts nearly 2 million people a year.

Those reforms include firing many of the museum’s top officials; rolling out a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance”; introducing new K-12 learning materials such as a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage”; and unveiling a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

The draft plans were visible on the laptop and in handwritten notes of a White House staffer who was riding a D.C.-area Metro train in late October. A nearby commuter took pictures of the materials and sent them to ProPublica reporters, who in turn verified the information. It’s unclear what kind of reception the plans have received inside the Trump White House. The staffer and White House did not respond to requests for comment for the story.

Also on Tuesday, Lonnie Bunch, the Smithsonian Institution’s outgoing leader, responded to ProPublica’s reporting in a message sent to employees. “The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in his letter. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”
Pingree was not the only member of Congress who responded to ProPublica’s reporting with a pledge to defend the Smithsonian’s independence.

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., said on social media that if he becomes chair of the Senate Rules Committee — which has jurisdiction over the Smithsonian — in the next Congress, “we will protect it from Trump’s interference and overreach.”
“The Smithsonian is NOT a federal agency, it is an independent, nonpartisan organization overseen by Congress – not the White House,” Padilla wrote.
Incoming Congressman Fred Wellman, a Democrat elected this month to represent the suburbs of St. Louis, responded even more forcefully to ProPublica’s reporting on social media.
The post Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul appeared first on ProPublica.

title_en: High levels of salmonella found in some products from nation’s biggest turkey producer
excerpt_en: Two years of inspections at four Butterball plants show rates far exceeding US averages in ground or chopped meat
body_en: Inspectors found salmonella bacteria in more than a third of ground or chopped turkey samples at slaughterhouses owned by Butterball, the US’s biggest turkey company, data shows.

The US Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) food safety and inspection service (FSIS) and some states conduct regular checks for salmonella and other bacteria in commercial poultry plants. Salmonella can live in the intestines of poultry, and it can cause nausea, diarrhea and even death in humans if meat is not cooked properly and then consumed.

This story is published in partnership with investigative journalists at the publication SourceMaterial, which analyzed fiscal year 2025 and 2026 FSIS inspection data provided by animal-rights campaign group Project Slingshot. SourceMaterial verified the data and found that ground or chopped turkey contamination rates from all Butterball’s slaughterhouses were well above the industry average.

Just under 43% of ground or chopped turkey sampled over the past year at four Butterball plants contained the pathogen. No contamination was identified in Butterball’s whole birds or ready-to-eat (cooked) products.

But at its Mount Olive factory in North Carolina, the nation’s biggest turkey slaughterhouse, FSIS inspectors found salmonella in 16 of 45 ground or chopped turkey samples tested at Mount Olive, or 36%. That’s well above the USDA’s acceptable limit for salmonella contamination in individual plants, which is 13.5%. A slaughterhouse does not face any fine if it exceeds this limit nor does it have to recall products. But the USDA does require it to explain how it is addressing the issue.

The high prevalence of salmonella is concerning because the Mount Olive plant processes 285,000 birds a week and sells raw ground turkey, burgers and sausages nationwide. The company supplies the three biggest US supermarkets – Walmart, Costco and Kroger – as well as fast-food companies.

A Butterball spokesperson said in response to the contamination data: “At Butterball, food safety is critically important, and we work diligently to ensure consumers can feel confident in the products they prepare and serve to family and friends. We continue to invest in new technologies, strengthen our processes, and work with food safety experts to advance our practices and reduce pathogens, including salmonella.”

They also said the company was taking part in a pilot program with FSIS “evaluating the cause of foodborne illness” and pointed out that none of the company’s pre-cooked products contained salmonella.

Alice Johnson, senior vice-president of food safety, quality and animal care at Butterball, said the company believes FSIS should measure the quantity of salmonella in samples, not simply whether or not it is present, although experts interviewed by SourceMaterial disagreed.

“Yes, having less harmful salmonella contamination is better than having more of it,” said Sarah Sorscher, director of regulatory affairs at the Center for Science in the Public Interest. “You know what is even better still? Having no salmonella in your food. That’s sadly not where we are right now.”

At Butterball’s main rival, Jennie-O, 7% of ground and chopped turkey samples tested positive for pathogens in the last year. A spokesperson for Jennie-O said that the company’s food-safety program was “robust” and noted that its results “compare favorably to industry averages and remain well below applicable regulatory performance standards”.
Sorscher explained that ground and chopped turkey might be prone to higher contamination because “every processing step is another opportunity for the meat to become contaminated”.

Tests also found evidence of drug-resistant superbugs. Two-thirds of samples taken from birds’ intestines across all of Butterball’s slaughterhouses in the fiscal year 2026 that contained salmonella and campylobacter (another pathogen that can sicken humans) showed strains resistant to at least one antibiotic. Doctors often use antibiotics to treat severe cases of both infections.
Butterball’s Johnson pointed out that the drug-resistance tests use samples from whole birds and so do not necessarily show “contamination in finished poultry products”.
The government data covered the entire US meat industry, showing an average 12% of samples contaminated with any pathogen and 33% of pathogens resistant to drugs.
“I don’t see how we can call our food system the safest in the world when we don’t have standards to prevent people from getting sick from eating the poultry,” said Sorscher.

Thomas Gremillion, director of food policy at the Consumer Federation of America, said salmonella contamination is worsened by fast line speeds at slaughterhouses. The Trump administration has allowed poultry processors to boost line speeds to kill more animals per minute.

Faster speeds make it harder “to keep the animal viscera and what’s in the digestive tract from getting on the meat”, he said. “Beyond just being disgusting, it’s a food safety risk because that’s where the pathogenic bacteria concentrate.”

And, said Dani Replogle, an attorney at the non-profit Food & Water Watch, faster production means “more antibiotics in feed and in water” – which is at odds with Donald Trump’s promise to get chemicals out of our food. He has yet to move to reduce antibiotic use in the food supply.

Each year, about 25,500 Americans are hospitalized after being exposed to salmonella and campylobacter, leading to 435 deaths, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In 2019, Butterball recalled almost 80,000lbs (36,000kg) of turkey products from Mount Olive after an outbreak of illness across two states likely caused by salmonella linked to the company’s products.

The number of samples detecting antibiotic-resistant bacteria were comparable at Butterball and Jennie-O. At Butterball’s slaughterhouses, 65% of positive samples were resistant to at least one antibiotic drug, compared with 61% at Jennie-O.

title_en: UK food inflation could hit 5% next year, Bank of England says
excerpt_en: Sharp rise expected as cost pressures mount, with experts factoring in energy price cap hike and potential impact of El Niño
body_en: Food price inflation in the UK could hit 5% next year, the Bank of England has said, despite rising less sharply than feared since the onset of the Iran war.

The deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told MPs on the cross-party Treasury select committee: “Food price inflation is coming in under what we expected [it] to be, and in fact under what the industry expected it to be.”

But she said the Bank expected food price inflation to rise sharply from the current level of about 1.3%. “We think that … it will go up to 3 to 5% in the middle of next year. I mean, obviously that’s quite uncertain, but that pressure is there,” Lombardelli said.
Related: Price rises gather pace in UK shops amid higher energy costs
Lombardelli was being questioned by MPs alongside other members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC).
The MPC raised interest rates by a quarter-point to 4% at its last meeting earlier this month to tackle above-target inflation, and suggested further action could be necessary.
Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said the MPC was also monitoring the potential impact of this year’s unusually large El Niño weather event on future food prices.
“There is uncertainty around this. You know, we still don’t know what the impact of this El Niño effect is going to be, for instance, because it will take time for it to manifest,” he said.
Surging oil and gas prices have pushed up the annual rate of inflation, which hit 3.6% last month, with the cost of petrol and diesel up by more than 33% over the past year.

But so far there have been fewer knock-on effects beyond energy prices. Food inflation has fallen well short of the peak above 17% seen in 2023, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exacerbated the supply squeeze as the global economy emerged from the Covid-19 pandemic.
Catherine Mann, an external member of the MPC who voted for a half-point increase this month, pointed to fierce competition in the food retail sector as a reason price rises had been constrained.
“We all go shopping ourselves. I can say that Aldi price match in my stores is apparent. Now, it wasn’t apparent four years ago. So that’s, I think, important,” she said.
Related: UK food prices on track to rise by 50% since start of cost of living crisis
Oil prices have fallen sharply since the Democratic party’s sweep in the US midterms brought hopes of an end to the Iran conflict, and as alternative sources of supply start to come onstream.
Bailey said if these lower prices continued, they would moderate the Bank’s predictions for UK inflation – which it had expected to peak at almost 5% next year.

“The prices are volatile … if these current prices were to stay what they are, the peak of inflation mechanically would be lower,” he said. However, Bailey and other MPC members underlined that some inflationary pressure for next year is already baked in – pointing to the 26% rise in the price cap for household energy bills due in January as an example.

The two-hour hearing underlined the divisions within the committee. The more dovish Swati Dhingra suggesting she saw this month’s rate rise as a one-off “insurance” measure, while Mann said she feared the MPC had undermined public confidence by failing to move more aggressively.
Dhingra compared the muted impact of rocketing oil and gas prices this year on the wider economy with the effects of the surge in 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine.
At a similar point in that year, the prices of 70% of goods included in the consumer price index had risen, she said – but just 20% of prices have reacted so far this year.
But Mann pointed out that inflation had now been consistently above the Bank’s 2% target for five years.

“If we let inflation expectations drift away from 2% in the longer term, then monetary policy is going to have to work harder, meaning a higher rate for longer,” she said, adding: “The optimal response is to hike more and sooner.” The MPC’s next rate-setting meeting is on 17 December.

title_en: Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing
excerpt_en: The post Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Michelle Urra for ProPublica When Oregon’s Housing Stability Council met by Zoom in early October, the state’s top housing official told the oversight board that she wanted to address a story ProPublica published that morning.

The story revealed that the official, Andrea Bell, hadn’t clearly disclosed her husband’s work for a small consulting firm that helps housing authorities develop apartments, sometimes with money from Bell’s agency. Nor had she notified Gov. Tina Kotek about it, something Oregon law requires of a governor’s appointee when an actual or potential conflict arises.

Council members, who award hundreds of millions of dollars in housing subsidies, affirmed their support for Bell, who told them she wanted to be clear: “None of the projects that are coming from the council impact my household income.”

Newly obtained records, however, show a clear financial connection between the council’s decisions and her husband’s employer. The records also show that Bell was personally involved in meetings and internal discussions about state funding of a large apartment project, Aloha 209th, which her husband’s employer is helping to develop.
Backers of the Aloha 209th project in Portland’s suburbs are seeking $17.5 million from the housing council, which receives funding recommendations from Bell’s agency.

JH Brawner, the consulting firm that employs Bell’s husband, Joshua Crites, will earn a $2 million fee from the housing authority in Washington County if the transaction closes. If not, JH Brawner gets nothing.

A separate project outside Portland, the Park Place apartments in Clackamas County, already received money through Oregon’s housing agency. Five months after Oregon awarded $36 million to the project in May 2025, Clackamas County’s housing authority paid JH Brawner a $2.4 million consulting fee, the new records show.
Like the Washington County contract, the one with Clackamas County says that if funding fell through for any reason and the project didn’t move forward, “no fee shall be due” to the firm.

JH Brawner said Crites, the firm’s director of strategic initiatives, has not worked on the Aloha 209th project but was one of five staffers assigned to Park Place. JH Brawner pays employees, including Crites, a fixed salary that is not tied to any project closing, according to managing director Zak de Gorgue.
Bell, executive director of Oregon Housing and Community Services, said in a statement that she is “committed to transparency, accountability, and compliance with state law.”

“At no point in my tenure as executive director have I used my position to influence or benefit myself or anyone related to me,” she said. “To be clear, I made no efforts to influence funding, and the Aloha 209 project has not received funding from OHCS and remains on the waitlist.”

Bell’s public agency sits in the middle of the state’s effort to combat a homelessness problem that is among the nation’s worst. Kotek, the governor, has made building more housing a pillar of her time in office. Oregon Housing and Community Services has distributed billions of state and federal dollars to subsidize the construction of apartments intended to have affordable rents.

Norman Williams, a law professor at Willamette University College of Law who teaches about government ethics, said Bell should have reported to the governor that she had a possible conflict and stayed out of any discussions about the projects her husband’s employer helped develop.
“It may all be an innocent mistake on her part,” Williams said, “but she knows who her husband is working for and she doesn’t report that. It makes it look like she’s trying to conceal this.”

De Gorgue said in a statement that the Aloha 209th project is still in development and the company had “no knowledge of Andrea Bell taking any action to move the project forward, nor has JH Brawner & Company engaged in any advocacy to secure funding approval” from Bell’s agency. Funding applications were submitted by the local housing authorities, not by JH Brawner.
“We have no indication, nor any reason to believe, that any project on which we have consulted has been the beneficiary of inappropriate influence,” de Gorgue said.
Separately, he said Clackamas and Washington counties chose JH Brawner as a consultant years before the company hired Crites in 2023.
Crites did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

After ProPublica asked Bell about her husband’s employment in September, she amended three years of ethics disclosure forms, explicitly naming JH Brawner as his employer. (The one time her state filings alluded to Crites’ job before that was in 2025, with a misspelling: “Spouse serves in an advisory role for a developmen.” It showed only the company’s street address, misspelled, and not its name.)

Bell also asked the Oregon Government Ethics Commission for a formal opinion about her potential conflict at the direction of Kotek’s staff. That evaluation was paused after the commission opened a preliminary review in response to a citizen complaint about her lack of disclosure. The preliminary review is ongoing.

ProPublica obtained the new details about Bell’s involvement through county contracts and emails to and from Bell, which were released under Oregon’s public records law. Bell’s agency initially said the emails would cost $612.50 to produce but eventually provided them for free. Washington County charged $364.25 for contracts, invoices and other documents.

Though backers say the Aloha 209th housing development is ready to be built, it’s on a waitlist to receive money from the state. Its turn is not likely to come until at least late 2028. By then, local officials worry that the delay will jeopardize its other funding sources and the project may need an even larger subsidy.

title_en: Nasa knocked an asteroid off course. New closeup photos shed light on aftermath
excerpt_en: Images of Dimorphos four years on from crash could help scientists design potential planetary defence system
body_en: Humanity may not yet have a means of fending off a Vogon constructor fleet – the destroyers of Earth in The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy – but its prospects of surviving an encounter with a rogue asteroid are looking considerably brighter.

Four years after Nasa deliberately slammed a spacecraft into a roughly 160-metre-wide asteroid called Dimorphos to knock it off course, scientists have released the first closeup images of the aftermath.

They suggest the asteroid now has one face flattened with a stadium-sized crater and is tumbling chaotically. Meanwhile, hundreds of previously unknown boulders encircle Dimorphos and its larger companion asteroid, Didymos.

As well as shedding new light on what happened to the asteroid after the collision, the images, captured by the European Space Agency’s (Esa) Hera spacecraft, could help scientists design more effective missions to deflect potentially hazardous space rocks in the future.

“Nasa’s Dart [Double Asteroid Redirection Test] mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid’s orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself,” said the Hera mission manager, Ian Carnelli, at Esa. “By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet.”
Nasa’s mission aimed to test-drive a planetary defence system that could prevent humanity from going the same way as the dinosaurs, should an asteroid or comet threaten Earth.

Neither Dimorphos nor its larger companion asteroid, Didymos, posed such a threat, but their movements provided scientists with a convenient means of assessing whether the strategy of trying to knock an asteroid off course might work.
On 26 September 2022, the roughly half-tonne Dart spacecraft ploughed into Dimorphos at more than 13,000mph, blasting a vast cloud of rocky debris into space.

Observations by telescopes on Earth revealed that the mission had succeeded in shortening the time it took Dimorphos to orbit Didymos by about 33 minutes. Before the collision, Nasa officials had said a change of 73 seconds or more would be considered a success.
But how much of the asteroid was displaced and precisely how it responded to the collision have remained open questions.

To investigate, Esa launched its Hera mission on 7 October 2024. After a two-year journey, the car-sized spacecraft reached the asteroid pair this month and has been surveying them from a distance of 15-18 miles (25-30km).

“Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape or stayed the same,” said Dr Patrick Michel, Hera principal investigator and director of research at the CNRS Côte d’Azur observatory in France. “Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once. The face struck by Dart has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid’s entire width.”
While the rest of Dimorphos appears to be relatively unchanged, the impact has also left Dimorphos “tumbling wildly in its orbit”, added Dr Michael Kueppers, the Esa’s Hera mission scientist.
“Another big surprise is that Hera is showing that the asteroids are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders, just a few metres in size,” Kueppers said.
Dr Michaël Marsset, an astronomer at the European Southern Observatory in Germany, described the release of the images as “a major milestone for both planetary defence and asteroid science”.

Unlike naturally occurring asteroid collisions, scientists knew precisely the mass, velocity and trajectory of the projectile and now had images of the asteroid before and after the impact, he said. “This offers a unique opportunity to study the physics of impacts at the scale of an asteroid.”
The Dart impact may also have exposed pristine material beneath Dimorphos’s weathered surface, offering scientists a rare glimpse of its interior, Marsset added.
Over the coming months, Hera will venture progressively closer to the asteroids and deploy two shoebox-sized satellites, one of which will use radar to peer inside Dimorphos.
The ultimate aim of these investigations is to transform asteroid deflection from a successful one-off experiment into a reliable means of planetary defence.

“The initial idea of deflecting an asteroid is not as straightforward as it sounds,” said Dr Ian Whittaker, a senior lecturer in physics at Nottingham Trent University. Although the momentum transferred by a spacecraft colliding with an asteroid should alter its motion, much also depends on how the asteroid responds to the impact, including how much material is blasted into space.“These images will help with understanding what is present after the impact and make for more accurate calculations in the future,” he said.

Asteroids are also remarkably diverse, ranging from relatively solid bodies to loose piles of rocks held together by their own weak gravity, said Marsset. “If we ever have to deflect another asteroid, this time on a collision course with Earth, we need to know what we are shooting at.”

The other major challenge is detecting potentially hazardous asteroids sufficiently early. Given years or decades of warning, even a tiny change in an asteroid’s velocity could be enough to make it miss Earth. “If it is discovered only months before impact, our options become considerably more limited,” Marsset said.

title_en: London Museum’s donors and the capital’s dubious domination | Letters
excerpt_en: Letters: Omitting to acknowledge the generosity of private donors risks reinforcing the widespread view that ‘magisterial’ civic amenities just happen by magic, writes Beth Breeze. Plus letters from Rendel Harris and Tom Uprichard
body_en: Oliver Wainwright’s extremely positive review of the “magisterial” new London Museum will encourage many to visit ( Take me to the fatberg! The £437m new Museum of London is an astonishing sight, 24 November).

But amid the praise for the architects who masterminded this transformation, and the well‑aimed barbs at the City of London Corporation, which tried to prevent it, there is no mention of those who provided the all-important funding. In particular, omitting to acknowledge the generosity of private donors risks reinforcing the widespread view that fantastic civic amenities just happen by magic, or are totally funded by taxpayers.

I encourage your readers to take a look at the lengthy list of philanthropic supporters – including historic charitable foundations, newly wealthy people, and our collective giving through the National Lottery – listed at www.londonmuseum.org.uk/support-us/our-supporters Beth Breeze Professor of philanthropy, Saïd Business School, University of Oxford

• Jonathan Jones, in his review of the new London Museum ( The reborn Museum of London is all piazza, no punch”, 24 November), confidently states: “For not since ancient Rome has a capital dominated its nation’s history and culture like London.” Paris, Vienna and Moscow, among others, would like a word. Rendel Harris London
• Did Oliver Wainwright go to the same London Museum as Jonathan Jones for their reviews? Tom Uprichard London
• Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title_en: Jensen Huang’s controversial return to Nvidia poses the question – what’s the point of a board?
excerpt_en: An independent board that isn’t able to fire a chief executive is just a cheer squad – not the umpire it’s supposed to be.
body_en: Patrick T. Fallon/Getty It’s hard to think of Nvidia without picturing Jensen Huang. Rarely seen without his signature black leather jacket, Huang has led chipmaker Nvidia since co-founding it in 1993, turning it into a central player in the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
Earlier this month, Huang resigned as president, chief executive officer and a member of Nvidia’s board, in the wake of a bombshell scandal involving affairs and alleged corporate espionage.
Days later, the board linked his departure to “personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”. It said it did “not intend to reinstate” him.
This week, however, it voted unanimously to bring him back, following a remarkable intervention by US President Donald Trump.
Many analysts have already weighed in on why the US government intervened. But there’s a deeper, more fundamental question here about corporate power.
If a chief executive is seen as too valuable to lose, can a company’s board still hold them to account? If it can’t, what exactly is the board for?
Read more: Trump had 4 reasons to ‘convince’ Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang. Here’s why it matters globally

The ‘key person risk’ Sometimes, the “ hero ” leader of a company can become its biggest vulnerability. In corporate governance, this is called “key person risk”. It is the danger a company comes to depend so heavily on one person that losing them would do serious damage.
This problem often grows out of success. A founder who builds a business and shapes its culture becomes its public face. Staff, customers and investors start to see the person and the company as one.
Think of Steve Jobs, co-founder and longtime chief executive of Apple, or even the fictional media magnate Logan Roy in the TV series Succession.

Nvidia itself recognised this risk before Huang’s brief removal. Its 2026 annual report warned the company was “highly dependent on the services” of its longstanding executive team, and that failing “to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions” could hinder its success in the long term.
Despite this, when Huang left, no permanent successor was ready. Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, stepped in temporarily while the board searched for a replacement.

Who’s watching the boss? So, what is a board actually for? Shareholders can’t supervise the managers in a large company like Nvidia; instead, they elect a board of directors to do it for them. While the board isn’t involved in daily operations of the company, it approves big decisions, watches the chief executive and, if needed, replaces them.
It’s designed to solve something economists call the “ principal-agent problem ”. A company’s managers (the agents) may put their own interests ahead of the owners’ (the principals).

That’s why independence matters. Independent directors don’t work for the company and have no close financial or personal ties to its management. Filling a board with the chief executive’s employees (such as other senior executives) and friends is like letting students mark their own exams.
Nvidia’s U-turn shows how fragile independence can be. A committee of independent directors is still investigating claims that Huang was targeted by China’s top spy agency.
Huang is also due to answer questions from US lawmakers behind closed doors on December 1. The board brought him back before either had finished.

The board acknowledged that its decision to rehire Huang was heavily influenced by the US government. It said it was “confident” Huang posed “no national security risk”, based on “input from senior US government levels”.

We have seen other boards cave under pressure before. In November 2023, OpenAI’s board fired its chief executive, Sam Altman. Within days, nearly all of its 770 staff threatened to quit. Altman returned, and the board that sacked him was replaced.

Independent of whom? On paper, there are strong safeguards to protect board independence. For example, the Nasdaq stock exchange, where Nvidia is listed, requires most directors to be independent. The committees that check a company’s accounts and set executive pay must be fully independent.
But these rules fall short in three ways.
First, the board itself gets to decide who counts as “independent”.

title_en: ‘It’s been really a mess’: Meta insiders concerned over push to AI content moderation
excerpt_en: Several employees say rapid speed at which algorithms work means mistakes can happen at greater scale
body_en: Meta employees have expressed concern at the company’s push to replace human moderators with artificial intelligence, claiming the technology is leading to mistakes with the potential for sweeping political consequences.
The social media company, which owns Facebook and Instagram, has been experimenting with AI-driven moderation for years, first introducing it in 2017 to filter out violent extremist content.
This March, Meta announced it was “transforming our approach” by rolling out “more advanced AI systems” to moderate content across its apps, framing the change as a way to improve enforcement.
Several Meta employees said that behind the scenes this push to AI was accompanied by mass layoffs across the company, severely affecting staff responsible for reviewing content on its platforms.
One described Meta’s content moderation as now operating with “skeleton teams”, some cut by at times half or two-thirds of their staff.
“It’s been really a mess,” they said, adding that on several recent occasions they had gone to discuss an issue with a specific content moderation team, only to find that entire team was now gone.

Meta has long sought inexpensive ways to moderate the vast volumes of content posted each day to its platforms. It has faced legal action from former outsourced content moderators in Kenya, who described struggling with PTSD and severe mental health issues after being paid as little as $1.50 (£1.13) an hour to view and evaluate extremely graphic content that users attempted to post.
Meta employees say AI systems that the company is now using struggle with nuance, especially in languages other than English, and frequently remove content that should not be taken down.

“You are trying to gut all human reviewers, which are kind of essential for making these nuanced decisions and policy decisions,” said one employee. “Of course there are going to be mistakes that are going to happen.”

The employee said that because algorithms were automated, and worked at greater speed than humans, these mistakes could happen at a greater scale. The employee said Meta was removing lower-paid contractors, such as those in Kenya, and the full-time employees who would handle more complex content moderation.

Once a post is taken down, there is far less recourse for the affected accounts than before. “Even if you know someone at Meta, it’s still very difficult to get through to someone who’s actually going to be able to help you, especially if it’s a highly nuanced case,” the employee said. “It’s so much more difficult now.”

The growth in AI moderation comes as researchers monitoring online censorship have noticed a new phenomenon: sudden restrictions on Instagram and Facebook accounts, often during pivotal political moments.

Some of these have been isolated occurrences, such as Meta’s suspension of the US No Kings account in the run-up to the US midterm elections. Others have amounted to “mass takedowns”, unfolding over the course of days and hitting dozens of social media accounts.

It is a growing phenomenon, the consequences of which could “shape the political future of entire nations”, said Martha Dimitratou, the founder of the group Repro Uncensored, which monitors digital censorship.

Repro Uncensored has tracked these takedowns in Brazil, the EU, Turkey and the US. The Guardian reported on a wave of account takedowns on Meta platforms late last year, affecting accounts posting queer content and those dedicated to reproductive health across Europe. Accounts backing the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, were restricted or suspended from Instagram in the feverish days of Brazil’s election runoff, according to Repro Uncensored. Meta said most of the Brazilian takedowns were to comply with valid court orders or electoral regulations.
The numbers of affected accounts appear to be rising: Repro Uncensored documented 210 incidents of account takedowns on Meta in 2025, and 657 in the first six months of 2026.

Meta employees who spoke to the Guardian said AI moderation had a role in such incidents as algorithms worked faster, and with less nuance, than human reviewers. “The effect of it is you see these sweeping takedowns,” one said.

But they also said they could not rule out political considerations in how Meta’s algorithm was designed. Meta’s systems are opaque, even to its employees. They are a combination of LLMs – large language models, like chatbots – and older algorithms that filter content.
There are “thousands of levers and factors that weigh into how things are ranked”, said one employee, and these change constantly.

The employees suggested that at times Meta’s use of AI had allowed the company to obscure more controversial decisions it makes in how it moderates political content. They gave the example of how Meta made adjustments to its algorithm in late 2023 that drastically limited the number of posts that appeared from people in Palestine.

The company rejected allegations of bias and said it had previously carried out independent human rights due diligence in relation to the conflict, and since 2022 had been working to implement the resultant recommendations, including by “introducing a system that detects and prioritises content to moderators most likely to understand that particular Arabic dialect”.
One employee said AI offered “plausible deniability”. It afforded “exactly the kind of ambiguity that they hide behind”, they said.

title_en: Climate summits need radical reform – here’s how to transform global negotiations
excerpt_en: The collapse of Cop31 may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems.
body_en: DENIS ESAULOV 1987/Shutterstock The recent failure of the UN climate summit, Cop31, went beyond already gloomy expectations. Yet this political and diplomatic catastrophe may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems.

It is a miracle that Cop climate summits have survived and grown for 31 years, with all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. Cops have produced some positive results such as the 2015 Paris climate agreement to cut greenhouse gases. But now it’s time for radical reform. A reform that must not only abolish unanimity, but also make the Cop capable of engaging a strong enough coalition of interests to advance the climate change agenda.
Where could that start? What kind of alliance does such a reform need? A recent conference on the global governance of climate change provides some answers.

Ending unanimity Cop has probably been killed by a contradiction. The first Cop in 1995 – chaired by Angela Merkel, then Germany’s young environment minister – was regulated by a UN law. This was the Framework Convention on Climate Change, which envisaged that decisions had to be taken by consensus or, if that wasn’t possible, by two-thirds of the parties (each state of the world is a “party”). This law, known as draft rule 42, was never accepted or rejected, leaving Cop trapped in the unanimity trap.

In 2010, this was enough for Bolivia alone to object to risk derailing the entire negotiation. It is a trap because countries have naturally different interests. Most developing countries are highly exposed to climate change and do not contribute much to the problem; some others not only benefit from oil production but also from global warming itself (notably Russia, as Arctic trade routes open up due to ice melting).

Most other traditional UN institutions do not operate under such strict consensus: the General Assembly (the main policymaking body of the UN), Unesco (the UN’s Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation) and the World Health Organization all vote with a qualified two-thirds majority on important matters.

So unanimity must be abolished. But that is not enough. Cop also manages to be both inefficient and not inclusive enough of the actors that matter a lot in achieving the goals of a climate change agenda. The parties include the tiny country of San Marino yet there’s no representation from megacities like Mumbai or Seattle – cities which may be exposed to climate disaster and host some of the solutions.

A new annual conference called Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was a significant attempt to move beyond the Cop gridlock. In 2026, 57 countries joined the first meeting in Santa Marta, Colombia after realising at Cop30 last year in Brazil, that, by “consensus”, Cop cannot even agree on the need for a roadmap to end dependence on fossil fuels. And yet even shrinking the number of parties to a quarter of Cop’s total was not enough to get beyond the acknowledgement of such a necessity: the final document did not indicate any timeline nor commit countries to specific targets.

The Cop climate negotiation process hinges on all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. metamorworks/Shutterstock It is too early to say that the Santa Marta process won’t work. But I would argue that it was a mistake not to invite certain nations, namely India and China and the US (although representatives from California did attend).

It was also risky to start the conference with a declaration ( issued by Colombia’s then president, Gustavo Petro about the inadequacy of capitalism to stop climate change. Capitalism may be a form of governing economy as primitive as fossil fuels, but to start from such a principle unnecessarily alienates leaders of other countries and business.

Coalition of the willing Another way to bring together countries and political sides that may have different visions of the world yet share common energy interests is to invite all countries that may respond positively to two simple questions: “Are you interested in developing within two years and sharing your plan to reduce in your country (or city or region) the percentage of energy consumption coming from fossil fuels? If so, are you willing to support each other in building the necessary supply chains and financial facilities to improve that target?”

This may inspire politically diverse local and national governments and business leaders to gradually join what would become a concrete problem-solving exercise. Common ground could hopefully be found in their shared interest to reduce energy dependency and mitigate climate risks.
Read more: What does climate adaptation actually mean? An expert explains

Once most of the net importers of fossil fuels are aligned, the net exporters (including some members of Opec, the oil producers’ cartel) may also commit. This is the sort of coalition of the willing that we need: an alliance capable of increasing its scope and delivering results.

As director of the thinktank Vision, I recently convened the fifth conference on global governance of climate change, held in Venice, Italy, in October 2026, titled Beyond Cop. Over three days, international delegates produced a strong proposal on how to reform Cop. The proposal was authored by professors and students including Kalypso Nikolaidis, chair in global affairs, and Helena Marchall, a masters student, both at the School of Transnational Governance of the European University Institute.

The conference proposes looking beyond ideologies, pre-defined agendas, cognitive biases and siloed thinking that make it difficult for politicians, business and academics to solve complex questions. One suggested change is to make Venice a permanent hub for a new global governance of climate adaptation (the practical steps to prepare for the consequences of a changing climate). This would help drive action and avoid the risk of focusing primarily on mitigation (cutting greenhouse gas emissions to achieve net zero).
